source.book: Accountancy : Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Summary: matters needing adjustment in the firm's books when a new partner is admitted.
cards.back:
goodwill
revaluation of assets and liabilities
reserves and other accumulated profits and losses
the capitals of the old partners' (if agreed)
cards.quote: Various matters which need adjustments in the books of firm at the time of admission of a new partner are : goodwill, revaluation of assets and liabilities, reserves and other accumulated profits and losses and the capitals of the old partners' (if agreed).

source.book: Accountancy : Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is ‘Financial Statement Analysis’?
cards.back: The process of critical evaluation of the financial information contained in the financial statements in order to understand and make decisions regarding the operations of the firm is called ‘Financial Statement Analysis’.
cards.quote: The process of critical evaluation of the financial information contained in the financial statements in order to understand and make decisions regarding the operations of the firm is called ‘Financial Statement Analysis’.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.1 Meaning of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.note: Critically evaluating the data in financial statements to understand the firm and decide about its operations.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What does the term ‘analysis’ mean in financial analysis?
cards.back: The term analysis means simplification of financial data by methodical classification given in the financial statements.
cards.quote: The term analysis means simplification of financial data by methodical classification given in the financial statements.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.1 Meaning of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What does ‘interpretation’ mean in financial analysis?
cards.back: Interpretation means explaining the meaning and significance of the data.
cards.quote: Interpretation means explaining the meaning and significance of the data.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.1 Meaning of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the two bases of comparison in financial analysis.
cards.back:
comparison with other firms (cross sectional analysis)
with firms' own performance, over a time period (time series analysis)
cards.quote: comparison with other firms (cross sectional analysis) and with firms' own performance, over a time period (time series analysis)

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.1 Meaning of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is financial analysis?
cards.back: Financial analysis is the process of identifying the financial strengths and weaknesses of the firm by properly establishing relationships between the various items of the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss.
cards.quote: Financial analysis is the process of identifying the financial strengths and weaknesses of the firm by properly establishing relationships between the various items of the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.note: Finding a firm's strengths and weaknesses by relating balance sheet and profit and loss items.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the parties that undertake financial analysis.
cards.back:
management of the firm
owners
trade creditors
lenders
investors
labour unions
analysts
others
cards.quote: Financial analysis can be undertaken by management of the firm, or by parties outside the firm, viz., owners, trade creditors, lenders, investors, labour unions, analysts and others.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Financial analysis helps the top management in which three ways?
cards.back:
measuring the success of the company's operations
appraising the individual's performance
evaluating the system of internal control
cards.quote: Financial analysis helps the management in measuring the success of the company's operations, appraising the individual's performance and evaluating the system of internal control.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Which position of the firm do trade payables evaluate through financial analysis?
cards.back: Their analysis will, therefore, evaluate the firm's liquidity position.
cards.quote: Their analysis will, therefore, evaluate the firm's liquidity position.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Suppliers of long-term debt are concerned with the firm's long-term ____ and survival.
cards.back: Suppliers of long-term debt are concerned with the firm's long-term solvency and survival.
cards.quote: Suppliers of long-term debt are concerned with the firm's long-term solvency and survival.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What do labour unions assess when they analyse the financial statements?
cards.back: Labour unions analyse the financial statements to assess whether it can presently afford a wage increase and whether it can absorb a wage increase through increased productivity or by raising the prices.
cards.quote: Labour unions analyse the financial statements to assess whether it can presently afford a wage increase and whether it can absorb a wage increase through increased productivity or by raising the prices.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: For what purposes do government agencies need financial analysis?
cards.back: The government agencies need it for price regulations, taxation and other similar purposes.
cards.quote: The government agencies need it for price regulations, taxation and other similar purposes.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.2 Significance of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the objectives of analysis of financial statements.
cards.back:
to assess the current profitability and operational efficiency of the firm as a whole as well as its different departments so as to judge the financial health of the firm.
to ascertain the relative importance of different components of the financial position of the firm.
to identify the reasons for change in the profitability/financial position of the firm.
to judge the ability of the firm to repay its debt and assessing the short-term as well as the long-term liquidity position of the firm.
cards.quote: to assess the current profitability and operational efficiency of the firm as a whole as well as its different departments so as to judge the financial health of the firm. to ascertain the relative importance of different components of the financial position of the firm. to identify the reasons for change in the profitability/financial position of the firm. to judge the ability of the firm to repay its debt and assessing the short-term as well as the long-term liquidity position of the firm.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.3 Objectives of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What must an analyst be conscious of while using financial analysis?
cards.back:
price level changes
window dressing of financial statements
changes in accounting policies of a firm
accounting concepts and conventions
personal judgement
cards.quote: the analyst must be conscious of the impact of price level changes, window dressing of financial statements, changes in accounting policies of a firm, accounting concepts and conventions, personal judgement, etc.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the limitations of financial analysis.
cards.back:
Financial analysis does not consider price level changes.
Financial analysis may be misleading without the knowledge of the changes in accounting procedure followed by a firm.
Financial analysis is just a study of reports of the company.
Monetary information alone is considered in financial analysis while non-monetary aspects are ignored.
The financial statements are prepared on the basis of accounting concept, as such, it does not reflect the current position.
cards.quote: 1. Financial analysis does not consider price level changes. 2. Financial analysis may be misleading without the knowledge of the changes in accounting procedure followed by a firm. 3. Financial analysis is just a study of reports of the company. 4. Monetary information alone is considered in financial analysis while non-monetary aspects are ignored. 5. The financial statements are prepared on the basis of accounting concept, as such, it does not reflect the current position.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the basic financial statements an annual report contains.
cards.back:
Balance Sheet
Statement of Profit and Loss
Cash Flow Statement
cards.quote: An annual report contains basic financial statements, viz., Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss and Cash Flow Statement.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the commonly used tools of financial analysis.
cards.back:
Comparative statements
Common size statement
trend analysis
ratio analysis
cash flow analysis
cards.quote: Commonly used tools of financial analysis are: Comparative statements, Common size statement, trend analysis, ratio analysis, and cash flow analysis.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What does the Position Statement show?
cards.back: Position Statement (showing the financial position of an enterprise as on a particular date)
cards.quote: Position Statement (showing the financial position of an enterprise as on a particular date)

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What does the Income Statement show?
cards.back: Income Statement (showing the result of the operational activities of an enterprise over a particular period)
cards.quote: Income Statement (showing the result of the operational activities of an enterprise over a particular period)

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: There is also a third important financial statement known as Cash flow statement, which shows ____ and outflows of the cash and cash equivalents.
cards.back: There is also a third important financial statement known as Cash flow statement, which shows inflows and outflows of the cash and cash equivalents.
cards.quote: There is also a third important financial statement known as Cash flow statement, which shows inflows and outflows of the cash and cash equivalents.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Accounting Standards are notified under section ____ of the Companies Act, 2013
cards.back: Accounting Standards are notified under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013
cards.quote: Accounting Standards are notified under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Which Accounting Standard governs the Cash Flow Statement under the Companies Act, 2013?
cards.back: includes Cash Flow Statement prepared in accordance with Accounting Standard- 3 (AS-3)- Cash Flow Statement.
cards.quote: includes Cash Flow Statement prepared in accordance with Accounting Standard- 3 (AS-3)- Cash Flow Statement.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.note: AS-3 is the accounting standard for the Cash Flow Statement.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is a Cash flow statement?
cards.back: A Cash flow statement shows inflow and outflow of cash and cash equivalents from various activities of a company during a specific period.
cards.quote: A Cash flow statement shows inflow and outflow of cash and cash equivalents from various activities of a company during a specific period.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is the primary objective of a cash flow statement?
cards.back: The primary objective of cash flow statement is to provide useful information about cash flows (inflows and outflows) of an enterprise during a particular period under various heads, i.e., operating activities, investing activities and financing activities.
cards.quote: The primary objective of cash flow statement is to provide useful information about cash flows (inflows and outflows) of an enterprise during a particular period under various heads, i.e., operating activities, investing activities and financing activities.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What basis does cash flow information give to users of financial statements?
cards.back: This information is useful in providing users of financial statements with a basis to assess the ability of the enterprise to generate cash and cash equivalents and the needs of the enterprise to utilise those cash flows.
cards.quote: This information is useful in providing users of financial statements with a basis to assess the ability of the enterprise to generate cash and cash equivalents and the needs of the enterprise to utilise those cash flows.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: For which periods should an enterprise present a cash flow statement?
cards.back: It requires that an enterprise should prepare a cash flow statement and should present it for each accounting period for which financial statements are presented.
cards.quote: It requires that an enterprise should prepare a cash flow statement and should present it for each accounting period for which financial statements are presented.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name four benefits of a cash flow statement.
cards.back:
enables users to evaluate changes in net assets of an enterprise, its financial structure (including its liquidity and solvency)
enables users to develop models to assess and compare the present value of the future cash flows of different enterprises
enhances the comparability of the reporting of operating performance by different enterprises
helps in balancing its cash inflow and cash outflow, keeping in response to changing condition
cards.quote: A cash flow statement when used along with other financial statements provides information that enables users to evaluate changes in net assets of an enterprise, its financial structure (including its liquidity and solvency) and its ability to affect the amounts and timings of cash flows in order to adapt to changing circumstances and opportunities.  Cash flow information is useful in assessing the ability of the enterprise to generate cash and cash equivalents and enables users to develop models to assess and compare the present value of the future cash flows of different enterprises.  It also enhances the comparability of the reporting of operating performance by different enterprises because it eliminates the effects of using different accounting treatments for the same transactions and events.  It also helps in balancing its cash inflow and cash outflow, keeping in response to changing condition. It is also helpful in checking the accuracy of past assessments of future cash flows and in examining the relationship between profitability and net cash flow and impact of changing prices.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is ‘Cash’ as per AS-3?
cards.back: As per AS-3, ‘Cash’ comprises cash in hand and demand deposits with banks
cards.quote: As per AS-3, ‘Cash’ comprises cash in hand and demand deposits with banks

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What are ‘Cash equivalents’ as per AS-3?
cards.back: ‘Cash equivalents’ means short-term highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value.
cards.quote: ‘Cash equivalents’ means short-term highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: An investment normally qualifies as cash equivalents only when it has a short maturity, of say, ____ or less from the date of acquisition.
cards.back: An investment normally qualifies as cash equivalents only when it has a short maturity, of say, three months or less from the date of acquisition.
cards.quote: An investment normally qualifies as cash equivalents only when it has a short maturity, of say, three months or less from the date of acquisition.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Investments in ____ are excluded from cash equivalents unless they are in substantial cash equivalents.
cards.back: Investments in shares are excluded from cash equivalents unless they are in substantial cash equivalents.
cards.quote: Investments in shares are excluded from cash equivalents unless they are in substantial cash equivalents.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Give NCERT's example of preference shares that qualify as cash equivalents.
cards.back: For example, preference shares of a company acquired shortly before their specific redemption date, provided there is only insignificant risk of failure of the company to repay the amount at maturity.
cards.quote: For example, preference shares of a company acquired shortly before their specific redemption date, provided there is only insignificant risk of failure of the company to repay the amount at maturity.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: How are short-term marketable securities that can be readily converted into cash treated?
cards.back: short-term marketable securities which can be readily converted into cash are treated as cash equivalents and is liquidable immediately without considerable change in value
cards.quote: short-term marketable securities which can be readily converted into cash are treated as cash equivalents and is liquidable immediately without considerable change in value

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What are ‘Cash Flows’?
cards.back: ‘Cash Flows’ implies movement of cash in and out due to some non-cash items.
cards.quote: ‘Cash Flows’ implies movement of cash in and out due to some non-cash items.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Receipt of cash from a non-cash item is termed as cash ____ while cash payment in respect of such items as cash ____.
cards.back: Receipt of cash from a non-cash item is termed as cash inflow while cash payment in respect of such items as cash outflow.
cards.quote: Receipt of cash from a non-cash item is termed as cash inflow while cash payment in respect of such items as cash outflow.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Is purchase of machinery for cash an inflow or outflow? And sale proceeds of machinery?
cards.back: For example, purchase of machinery by paying cash is cash outflow while sale proceeds received from sale of machinery is cash inflow.
cards.quote: For example, purchase of machinery by paying cash is cash outflow while sale proceeds received from sale of machinery is cash inflow.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Cash management includes the investment of ____ in cash equivalents.
cards.back: Cash management includes the investment of excess cash in cash equivalents.
cards.quote: Cash management includes the investment of excess cash in cash equivalents.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Is purchase of marketable securities that are cash equivalents shown in the cash flow statement?
cards.back: Hence, purchase of marketable securities or short-term investment which constitutes cash equivalents is not considered while preparing cash flow statement.
cards.quote: Hence, purchase of marketable securities or short-term investment which constitutes cash equivalents is not considered while preparing cash flow statement.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: As per AS-3, how are activities classified for a cash flow statement?
cards.back: (1) operating, (2) investing, and (3) financing activities
cards.quote: these activities are to be classified into three categories: (1) operating, (2) investing, and (3) financing activities

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 6.5 Classification of Activities for the Preparation of Cash Flow Statement

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What are operating activities?
cards.back: Operating activities are the activities that constitute the primary or main activities of an enterprise.
cards.quote: Operating activities are the activities that constitute the primary or main activities of an enterprise.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Give NCERT's example of operating activities for a garment manufacturing company.
cards.back: For example, for a company manufacturing garments, operating activities are procurement of raw material, incurrence of manufacturing expenses, sale of garments, etc.
cards.quote: For example, for a company manufacturing garments, operating activities are procurement of raw material, incurrence of manufacturing expenses, sale of garments, etc.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: The amount of cash from operations’ indicates the internal ____ level of the company
cards.back: The amount of cash from operations’ indicates the internal solvency level of the company
cards.quote: The amount of cash from operations’ indicates the internal solvency level of the company

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the cash inflows from operating activities.
cards.back:
cash receipts from sale of goods and the rendering of services.
cash receipts from royalties, fees, commissions and other revenues.
cards.quote: Cash Inflows from operating activities cash receipts from sale of goods and the rendering of services. cash receipts from royalties, fees, commissions and other revenues.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is cash flow analysis?
cards.back: It refers to the analysis of actual movement of cash into and out of an organisation.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.4 Tools of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the cash outflows from operating activities.
cards.back:
Cash payments to suppliers for goods and services.
Cash payments to and on behalf of the employees.
Cash payments to an insurance enterprise for premiums and claims, annuities, and other policy benefits.
Cash payments of income taxes unless they can be specifically identified with financing and investing activities.
cards.quote: Cash Outflows from operating activities Cash payments to suppliers for goods and services. Cash payments to and on behalf of the employees. Cash payments to an insurance enterprise for premiums and claims, annuities, and other policy benefits. Cash payments of income taxes unless they can be specifically identified with financing and investing activities.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: The flow of cash into the business is called as cash inflow or ____
cards.back: The flow of cash into the business is called as cash inflow or positive cash flow
cards.quote: The flow of cash into the business is called as cash inflow or positive cash flow

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.4 Tools of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is the flow of cash out of the firm called?
cards.back:
Cash outflow or a negative cash flow
the flow of cash out of the firm is called as cash outflow or a negative cash flow.
cards.quote: the flow of cash out of the firm is called as cash outflow or a negative cash flow.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.4 Tools of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: How are cash flows from purchase and sale of dealing or trading securities classified?
cards.back: cash flows arising from the purchase and sale of dealing or trading securities are classified as operating activities
cards.quote: cash flows arising from the purchase and sale of dealing or trading securities are classified as operating activities

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: How are cash advances and loans made by financial enterprises classified?
cards.back: cash advances and loans made by financial enterprises are usually classified as operating activities since they relate to main activity of that enterprise.
cards.quote: cash advances and loans made by financial enterprises are usually classified as operating activities since they relate to main activity of that enterprise.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: The difference between the inflow and outflow of cash is the ____.
cards.back: The difference between the inflow and outflow of cash is the net cash flow.
cards.quote: The difference between the inflow and outflow of cash is the net cash flow.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 4.4 Tools of Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What are investing activities as per AS-3?
cards.back: As per AS-3, investing activities are the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and other investments not included in cash equivalents.
cards.quote: As per AS-3, investing activities are the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and other investments not included in cash equivalents.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Transactions related to ____ investment are also investing activities.
cards.back: Transactions related to long-term investment are also investing activities.
cards.quote: Transactions related to long-term investment are also investing activities.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the cash outflows from investing activities.
cards.back:
Cash payments to acquire fixed assets including intangibles and capitalised research and development.
Cash payments to acquire shares, warrants or debt instruments of other enterprises other than the instruments those held for trading purposes.
Cash advances and loans made to third party (other than advances and loans made by a financial enterprise wherein it is operating activities).

Cash payments to acquire shares, warrants or debt instruments of other enterprises other than the instruments those held for trading purposes. Cash advances and loans made to third party (other than advances and loans made by a financial enterprise wherein it is operating activities).

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the cash inflows from investing activities.

Cash receipt from disposal of fixed assets including intangibles.

Cash receipt from disposal of shares, warrants or debt instruments of other enterprises except those held for trading purposes.
Interest received in cash from loans and advances.
Dividend received from investments in other enterprises.

Cash receipt from the repayment of advances or loans made to third parties (except in case of financial enterprise). Cash receipt from disposal of shares, warrants or debt instruments of other enterprises except those held for trading purposes. Interest received in cash from loans and advances. Dividend received from investments in other enterprises.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What are financing activities as per AS-3?
cards.back: As per AS-3, financing activities are activities that result in changes in the size and composition of the owners’ capital (including preference share capital in case of a company) and borrowings of the enterprise.
cards.quote: As per AS-3, financing activities are activities that result in changes in the size and composition of the owners’ capital (including preference share capital in case of a company) and borrowings of the enterprise.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Give NCERT's examples of financing activities.
cards.back: financing activities relate to long-term funds or capital of an enterprise, e.g., cash proceeds from issue of equity shares, debentures, raising long-term bank loans, repayment of bank loan, etc.
cards.quote: financing activities relate to long-term funds or capital of an enterprise, e.g., cash proceeds from issue of equity shares, debentures, raising long-term bank loans, repayment of bank loan, etc.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the cash inflows from financing activities.
cards.back:
Cash proceeds from issuing shares (equity or/and preference).
Cash proceeds from issuing debentures, loans, bonds and other short/ long-term borrowings.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the cash outflows from financing activities.
cards.back:
Cash repayments of amounts borrowed.
Interest paid on debentures and long-term loans and advances.

cards.front: How does AS-3 require cash flows from taxes on income to be classified?

cards.back: Therefore, the increase in current assets and decrease in current liabilities are deducted from the operating profit, and the decrease in current assets and increase in current liabilities are added to the operating profit so as to arrive at the exact amount of net cash flow from operating activities.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Under the indirect method (AS-3), net profit or loss is adjusted for the effect of which items?
cards.back:
Non-cash items such as depreciation, goodwill written-off, provisions, deferred taxes, etc., which are to be added back.
All other items for which the cash effects are investing or financing cash flows.
Changes in current assets and liabilities during the period.
cards.quote: As per AS-3, under indirect method, net cash flow from operating activities is determined by adjusting net profit or loss for the effect of : Non-cash items such as depreciation, goodwill written-off, provisions, deferred taxes, etc., which are to be added back. All other items for which the cash effects are investing or financing cash flows. The treatment of such items depends upon their nature. All investing and financing incomes are to be deducted from the amount of net profits while all such expenses are to be added back. For example, finance cost which is a financing cash outflow is to be added back while other income such as interest received which is investing cash inflow is to be deducted from the amount of net profit. Dividend declared is a financial activity and is therefore added back to net profit and shown as out flow under financial activity. Changes in current assets and liabilities during the period. Increase in current assets and decrease in current liabilities are to be deducted while increase in current liabilities and decrease in current assets are to be added up.

cards.quote: these statements refer to the statement of profit and loss and the balance sheet prepared by providing columns for the figures for both the current year as well as for the previous year and for the changes during the year, both in absolute and relative terms.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Steps in preparing comparative statements, in order.
cards.back:
Step 1 : List out absolute figures in rupees relating to two points of time (as shown in columns 2 and 3 of Exhibit 4.1).
Step 2 : Find out change in absolute figures by subtracting the first year (Col.2) from the second year (Col.3) and indicate the change as increase (+) or decrease (–) and put it in column 4.
Step 3 : Preferably, also calculate the percentage change as follows and put it in column 5.
cards.quote: Step 1 : List out absolute figures in rupees relating to two points of time (as shown in columns 2 and 3 of Exhibit 4.1). Step 2 : Find out change in absolute figures by subtracting the first year (Col.2) from the second year (Col.3) and indicate the change as increase (+) or decrease (–) and put it in column 4. Step 3 : Preferably, also calculate the percentage change as follows and put it in column 5.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Formula: percentage increase or decrease in a comparative statement.
cards.back: Absolute Increase or Decrease (Col.4) × 100 / First year absolute figure (Col.2)
cards.quote: Absolute Increase or Decrease (Col.4) × 100 / First year absolute figure (Col.2)

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.note: Percentage change = (change in Col.4 ÷ first-year figure in Col.2) × 100.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: By what other name is a common size statement also known?
cards.back:
Component percentage statement
Common Size Statement, also known as component percentage statement, is a financial tool for studying the key changes and trends in the financial position and operational result of a company.
cards.quote: Common Size Statement, also known as component percentage statement, is a financial tool for studying the key changes and trends in the financial position and operational result of a company.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: For example, a common size balance sheet shows the percentage of each asset to the ____, and that of each liability to the total liabilities.
cards.back: For example, a common size balance sheet shows the percentage of each asset to the total assets, and that of each liability to the total liabilities.
cards.quote: For example, a common size balance sheet shows the percentage of each asset to the total assets, and that of each liability to the total liabilities.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Similarly, in the common size statement of profit and loss, the items of expenditure are shown as a percentage of the ____.
cards.back: Similarly, in the common size statement of profit and loss, the items of expenditure are shown as a percentage of the revenue from operations.
cards.quote: Similarly, in the common size statement of profit and loss, the items of expenditure are shown as a percentage of the revenue from operations.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Steps in preparing common size statements, in order.
cards.back:
List out absolute figures in rupees at two points of time, say year 1, and year 2 (Column 2 & 4 of Exhibit 4.2).
Choose a common base (as 100). For example, revenue from operations may be taken as base (100) in case of statement of profit and loss and total assets or total liabilities (100) in case of balance sheet.
For all items of Col. 2 and 3 work out the percentage of that total. Column 4 and 5 shows these percentages in Exhibit 4.2.
cards.quote: 1. List out absolute figures in rupees at two points of time, say year 1, and year 2 (Column 2 & 4 of Exhibit 4.2). 2. Choose a common base (as 100). For example, revenue from operations may be taken as base (100) in case of statement of profit and loss and total assets or total liabilities (100) in case of balance sheet. 3. For all items of Col. 2 and 3 work out the percentage of that total. Column 4 and 5 shows these percentages in Exhibit 4.2.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is taken as the common base (100) in a common size statement of profit and loss and in a balance sheet?
cards.back: revenue from operations may be taken as base (100) in case of statement of profit and loss and total assets or total liabilities (100) in case of balance sheet.
cards.quote: revenue from operations may be taken as base (100) in case of statement of profit and loss and total assets or total liabilities (100) in case of balance sheet.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: State what a comparative statement shows (chapter summary).
cards.back: Comparative statement shows changes in all items of financial statements in absolute and percentage terms over a period of time for a firm or between two firms.
cards.quote: Comparative statement shows changes in all items of financial statements in absolute and percentage terms over a period of time for a firm or between two firms.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What does a common size statement express?
cards.back: Common size statement expresses all items of a financial statement as a percentage of some common base such as revenue from operations for statement of profit and loss and total assets for balance sheet.
cards.quote: Common size statement expresses all items of a financial statement as a percentage of some common base such as revenue from operations for statement of profit and loss and total assets for balance sheet.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: The finances raised through debentures are also known as ____.
cards.back: The finances raised through debentures are also known as long-term debt.
cards.quote: The finances raised through debentures are also known as long-term debt.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What is a debenture?
cards.back: Debenture is a written instrument acknowledging a debt under the common seal of the company.
cards.quote: Debenture is a written instrument acknowledging a debt under the common seal of the company.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What does ‘Debenture’ include under section 2(30) of The Companies Act, 2013?
cards.back: ‘Debenture’ includes Debenture Inventory, Bonds and any other securities of a company whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not.
cards.quote: According to section 2(30) of The Companies Act, 2013 ‘Debenture’ includes Debenture Inventory, Bonds and any other securities of a company whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What is a bond?
cards.back: Bond is also an instrument of acknowledgement of debt.
cards.quote: Bond is also an instrument of acknowledgement of debt.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: The terms ‘debentures’ and ‘Bonds’ are now being used ____.
cards.back: The terms ‘debentures’ and ‘Bonds’ are now being used inter-changeably.
cards.quote: The terms ‘debentures’ and ‘Bonds’ are now being used inter-changeably.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares vs debentures: the difference on ownership.
cards.back: A ‘share’ represents ownership of the company whereas a debenture is only acknowledgement of Debt. A share is a part of the owned capital whereas a debenture is a part of borrowed capital.
cards.quote: A ‘share’ represents ownership of the company whereas a debenture is only acknowledgement of Debt. A share is a part of the owned capital whereas a debenture is a part of borrowed capital.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares vs debentures: the difference on return.
cards.back: The return on shares is known as dividend while the return on debentures is called interest. The rate of return on shares may vary from year to year depending upon the profits of the company but the rate of interest on debentures is prefixed.
cards.quote: The return on shares is known as dividend while the return on debentures is called interest. The rate of return on shares may vary from year to year depending upon the profits of the company but the rate of interest on debentures is prefixed.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Dividend vs interest: how each is treated against profits.
cards.back: The payment of dividend is an appropriation of profits, whereas the payment of interest is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit.
cards.quote: The payment of dividend is an appropriation of profits, whereas the payment of interest is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares vs debentures: the difference on repayment.
cards.back: Normally, the amount of shares is not returned during the life of the company, whereas, generally, the debentures are issued for a specified period and repayable on the expiry of that period.
cards.quote: Normally, the amount of shares is not returned during the life of the company, whereas, generally, the debentures are issued for a specified period and repayable on the expiry of that period.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares vs debentures: the difference on voting rights.
cards.back: Shareholders enjoy voting rights whereas debentureholders do not normally enjoy any voting right.
cards.quote: Shareholders enjoy voting rights whereas debentureholders do not normally enjoy any voting right.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares vs debentures: the difference on security.
cards.back: Shares are not secured by any charge whereas the debentures are generally secured and carry a fixed or floating charge over the assets of the company.
cards.quote: Shares are not secured by any charge whereas the debentures are generally secured and carry a fixed or floating charge over the assets of the company.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares vs debentures: the difference on convertibility.
cards.back: Shares cannot be converted into debentures whereas debentures can be converted into shares if the terms of issue so provide, and in that case these are known as convertible debentures.
cards.quote: Shares cannot be converted into debentures whereas debentures can be converted into shares if the terms of issue so provide, and in that case these are known as convertible debentures.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Types of debentures.
cards.back:
secured and unsecured debentures
redeemable and perpetual debentures
convertible and non-convertible debentures
zero coupon rate and specific rate
registered and bearer debentures
cards.quote: Debentures are of various types such as: secured and unsecured debentures redeemable and perpetual debentures, convertible and non-convertible debentures, zero coupon rate and specific rate, registered and bearer debentures.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are secured debentures?
cards.back: Secured debentures refer to those debentures where a charge is created on the assets of the company for the purpose of payment in case of default. The charge may be fixed or floating.
cards.quote: Secured debentures refer to those debentures where a charge is created on the assets of the company for the purpose of payment in case of default. The charge may be fixed or floating.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.1 From the Point of view of Security

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: The fixed charge is created against those assets which are held by a company for use in operations ____
cards.back: The fixed charge is created against those assets which are held by a company for use in operations not meant for sale
cards.quote: The fixed charge is created against those assets which are held by a company for use in operations not meant for sale

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.1 From the Point of view of Security

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Floating charge: which assets does it involve?
cards.back:
All assets excluding those assigned to the secured creditors
The fixed charge is created against those assets which are held by a company for use in operations not meant for sale whereas floating charge involves all assets excluding those assigned to the secured creditors.
cards.quote: The fixed charge is created against those assets which are held by a company for use in operations not meant for sale whereas floating charge involves all assets excluding those assigned to the secured creditors.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.1 From the Point of view of Security

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are unsecured debentures?
cards.back: Unsecured debentures do not have a specific charge on the assets of the company.
cards.quote: Unsecured debentures do not have a specific charge on the assets of the company.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.1 From the Point of view of Security

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are redeemable debentures?
cards.back: Redeemable debentures are those which are payable on the expiry of the specific period either in lump sum or in Instalments during the life time of the company.
cards.quote: Redeemable debentures are those which are payable on the expiry of the specific period either in lump sum or in Instalments during the life time of the company.

source.section: 2.3.2 From the Point of view of Tenure

cards.front: Debentures can be redeemed either at ____ or at ____.
cards.back: Debentures can be redeemed either at par or at premium.
cards.quote: Debentures can be redeemed either at par or at premium.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.2 From the Point of view of Tenure

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are irredeemable debentures (also called Perpetual Debentures)?
cards.back: Irredeemable debentures are also known as Perpetual Debentures because the company does not give any undertaking for the repayment of money borrowed by issuing such debentures.
cards.quote: Irredeemable debentures are also known as Perpetual Debentures because the company does not give any undertaking for the repayment of money borrowed by issuing such debentures.

source.section: 2.3.2 From the Point of view of Tenure

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Irredeemable (Perpetual) debentures: when are they repayable?
cards.back:
On the winding-up of the company, or on the expiry of a long period
These debentures are repayable on the winding-up of a company or on the expiry of a long period.
cards.quote: These debentures are repayable on the winding-up of a company or on the expiry of a long period.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.2 From the Point of view of Tenure

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are convertible debentures?
cards.back: Debentures which are convertible into equity shares or in any other security either at the option of the company or the debentureholders are called convertible debentures.
cards.quote: Debentures which are convertible into equity shares or in any other security either at the option of the company or the debentureholders are called convertible debentures.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.3 From the Point of view of Convertibility

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are non-convertible debentures?
cards.back: The debentures which cannot be converted into shares or in any other securities are called non-convertible debentures.
cards.quote: The debentures which cannot be converted into shares or in any other securities are called non-convertible debentures.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 2.3.3 From the Point of view of Convertibility

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are specific coupon rate debentures?
cards.back: These debentures are issued with a specified rate of interest, which is called the coupon rate.
cards.quote: These debentures are issued with a specified rate of interest, which is called the coupon rate.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.back: The floating interest rate is usually tagged with the bank rate.
cards.quote: The floating interest rate is usually tagged with the bank rate.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are zero coupon rate debentures?
cards.back: These debentures do not carry a specific rate of interest. In order to compensate the investors, such debentures are issued at substantial discount and the difference between the nominal value and the issue price is treated as the amount of interest related to the duration of the debentures.
cards.quote: These debentures do not carry a specific rate of interest. In order to compensate the investors, such debentures are issued at substantial discount and the difference between the nominal value and the issue price is treated as the amount of interest related to the duration of the debentures.

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What are registered debentures?
cards.back: Registered debentures are those debentures in respect of which all details including names, addresses and particulars of holding of the debentureholders are entered in a register kept by the company. Such debentures can be transferred only by executing a regular transfer deed.
cards.quote: Registered debentures are those debentures in respect of which all details including names, addresses and particulars of holding of the debentureholders are entered in a register kept by the company. Such debentures can be transferred only by executing a regular transfer deed.

cards.back: Bearer debentures are the debentures which can be transferred by way of delivery and the company does not keep any record of the debentures

cards.front: Whole business taken over: if debentures issued exceed the net assets taken over, how is the excess treated?

cards.quote: According to Section 39 of the partnership Act 1932, the dissolution of partnership between all the partners of a firm is called the dissolution of the firm.

source.book: Accountancy Part 1 (Partnership Accounts)

cards.note: Dissolution of the firm means the partnership between all the partners ends.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: When a partnership is reconstituted by admission, retirement or death, what is dissolved and what is not?
cards.back: In such a situation while the existing partnership is dissolved, the firm may continue under the same name if the partners so decide. In other words, it results in the dissolution of a partnership but not that of the firm.
cards.quote: In such a situation while the existing partnership is dissolved, the firm may continue under the same name if the partners so decide. In other words, it results in the dissolution of a partnership but not that of the firm.

source.book: Accountancy Part 1 (Partnership Accounts)

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the 7 ways in which dissolution of partnership may take place.
cards.back:
(1) Change in existing profit sharing ratio among partners
(2) Admission of a new partner
(3) Retirement of a partner
(4) Death of a partner
(5) Insolvency of a partner
(6) Completion of the venture, if partnership is formed for that
(7) Expiry of the period of partnership, if partnership is for a specific period of time
cards.quote: The dissolution of partnership may take place in any of the following ways: (1) Change in existing profit sharing ratio among partners; (2) Admission of a new partner; (3) Retirement of a partner; (4) Death of a partner; (5) Insolvency of a partner; (6) Completion of the venture, if partnership is formed for that; and (7) Expiry of the period of partnership, if partnership is for a specific period of time;

source.book: Accountancy Part 1 (Partnership Accounts)

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Which dissolution necessarily brings the other: of the firm or of the partnership?
cards.back: It may be noted that dissolution of the firm necessarily brings in dissolution of the partnership. However, dissolution of partnership would not necessarily involve dissolution of firms.
cards.quote: It may be noted that dissolution of the firm necessarily brings in dissolution of the partnership. However, dissolution of partnership would not necessarily involve dissolution of firms.

cards.front: Types: the 5 ways in which dissolution of a firm takes place.
cards.back:
Dissolution by Agreement
Compulsory Dissolution
On the happening of certain contingencies
Dissolution by Notice
Dissolution by Court
cards.quote: Dissolution of a firm takes place in any of the following ways: 1. Dissolution by Agreement: A firm is dissolved : (a) with the consent of all the partners or (b) in accordance with a contract between the partners. 2. Compulsory Dissolution: A firm is dissolved compulsorily in the following cases: (a) when all the partners or all but one partner, become insolvent, rendering them incompetent to sign a contract; (b) when the business of the firm becomes illegal; or (c) when some event has taken place which makes it unlawful for the partners to carry on the business of the firm in partnership, e.g., when a partner who is a citizen of a country becomes an alien enemy because of the declaration of war with his country and India. 3. On the happening of certain contingencies: Subject to contract between the partners, a firm is dissolved : (a) if constituted for a fixed term, by the expiry of that term; (b) if constituted to carry out one or more ventures, by the completion thereof; (c) by the death of a partner; (d) by the adjudication of a partner as an insolvent. 4. Dissolution by Notice: In case of partnership at will, the firm may be dissolved if any one of the partners gives a notice in writing to the other partners, signifying his intention of seeking dissolution of the firm. 5. Dissolution by Court:

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the six specific objectives of financial statements.
cards.back:
1. To provide information about economic resources and obligations of a business
2. To provide information about the earning capacity of the business
3. To provide information about cash flows
4. To judge effectiveness of management
5. Information about activities of business affecting the society
6. Disclosing accounting policies
cards.quote: The specific objectives include the following: 1. To provide information about economic resources and obligations of a business: They are prepared to provide adequate, reliable and periodical information about economic resources and obligations of a business firm to investors and other external parties who have limited authority, ability or resources to obtain information. 2. To provide information about the earning capacity of the business: They are to provide useful financial information which can gainfully be utilised to predict, compare and evaluate the business firm’s earning capacity. 3. To provide information about cash flows: They are to provide information useful to investors and creditors for predicting, comparing and evaluating, potential cash flows in terms of amount, timing and related uncertainties. 4. To judge effectiveness of management: They supply information useful for judging management’s ability to utilise the resources of a business effectively. 5. Information about activities of business affecting the society: They have to report the activities of the business organisation affecting the society, which can be determined and described or measured and which are important in its social environment. 6. Disclosing accounting policies: These reports have to provide the significant policies, concepts followed in the process of accounting and changes taken up in them during the year to understand these statements in a better way.

source.book: Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

source.section: 3.5 Uses and Importance of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the seven uses and importance of financial statements.
cards.back:
1. Report on stewardship function
2. Basis for fiscal policies
3. Basis for granting of credit
4. Basis for prospective investors
5. Guide to the value of the investment already made
6. Aids trade associations in helping their members
7. Helps stock exchanges
cards.quote: The various uses and importance of financial statements are as follows: 1. Report on stewardship function: Financial statements report the performance of the management to the shareholders. The gaps between the management performance and ownership expectations can be understood with the help of financial statements. 2. Basis for fiscal policies: The fiscal policies, particularly taxation policies of the government, are related with the financial performance of corporate undertakings. The financial statements provide basic input for industrial, taxation and other economic policies of the government. 3. Basis for granting of credit: Corporate undertakings have to borrow funds from banks and other financial institutions for different purposes. Credit granting institutions take decisions based on the financial performance of the undertakings. Thus, financial statements form the basis for granting of credit. 4. Basis for prospective investors: The investors include both short-term and long-term investors. Their prime considerations in their investment decisions are security and liquidity of their investment with reasonable profitability. Financial statements help the investors to assess long-term and short-term solvency as well as the profitability of the concern. 5. Guide to the value of the investment already made: Shareholders of companies are interested in knowing the status, safety and return on their investment. They may also need information to take decision about continuation or discontinuation of their investment in the business. Financial statements provide information to the shareholders in taking such important decisions. 6. Aids trade associations in helping their members: Trade associations may analyse the financial statements for the purpose of providing service and protection to their members. cards.front: Name the 5 main factors affecting the value of goodwill.

1. Nature of business: A firm that produces high value added products or having a stable demand is able to earn more profits and therefore has more goodwill.
2. Location: If the business is centrally located or is at a place having heavy customer traffic, the goodwill tends to be high.
3. Efficiency of management: A well-managed concern usually enjoys the advantage of high productivity and cost efficiency.
4. Market situation: The monopoly condition or limited competition enables the concern to earn high profits which leads to higher value of goodwill.
5. Special advantages
cards.quote: The main factors affecting the value of goodwill are as follows: 1. Nature of business: A firm that produces high value added products or having a stable demand is able to earn more profits and therefore has more goodwill. 2. Location: If the business is centrally located or is at a place having heavy customer traffic, the goodwill tends to be high. 3. Efficiency of management: A well-managed concern usually enjoys the advantage of high productivity and cost efficiency. This leads to higher profits and so the value of goodwill will also be high. 4. Market situation: The monopoly condition or limited competition enables the concern to earn high profits which leads to higher value of goodwill. 5. Special advantages: The firm that enjoys special advantages like import licences, low rate and assured supply of electricity, long-term contracts for supply of materials, well-known collaborators, patents, trademarks, etc. enjoy higher value of goodwill.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the 6 essential features of partnership.
cards.back:
Two or More Persons
Agreement
Business
Mutual Agency
Sharing of Profit
Liability of Partners
cards.quote: Thus, the essential features of partnership are: 1. Two or More Persons: In order to form partnership, there should be at least two persons coming together for a common goal. In other words, the minimum number of partners in a firm can be two. There is however, a limit on their maximum number. By virtue of Section 464 of the Companies Act 2013, the Central Government is empowered to prescribe maximum number of partners in a firm but the number of partners can not be more than 100. The Central government has prescribed the maximum number of partness in a firm to be 50. 2. Agreement: Partnership is the result of an agreement between two or more persons to do business and share its profits and losses. The agreement becomes the basis of relationship between the partners. It is not necessary that such agreement is in written form. An oral agreement is equally valid. But in order to avoid disputes, it is preferred that the partners have a written agreement. 3. Business: The agreement should be to carry on some business. Mere co-ownership of a property does not amount to partnership. For example, if Rohit and Sachin jointly purchase a plot of land, they become the joint owners of the property and not the partners. But if they are in the business of purchase and sale of land for the purpose of making profit, they will be called partners. 4. Mutual Agency: The business of a partnership concern may be carried on by all the partners or any of them acting for all. This statement has two important implications. First, every partner is entitled to participate in the conduct of the affairs of its business. Second, that there exists a relationship of mutual agency between all the partners. Each partner carrying on the business is the principal as well as the agent for all the other partners. He can bind other partners by his acts and also is bound by the acts of other partners with regard to business of the firm. Relationship of mutual agency is so important that one can say that there would be no partnership, if the element of mutual agency is absent. 5. Sharing of Profit: Another important element of partnership is that, the agreement between partners must be to share profits and losses of a business. Though the definition contained in the Partnership Act describes partnership as relation between people who agree to share the profits of a business, the sharing of loss is implied. Thus, sharing of profits and losses is important. If some persons join hands for the purpose of some charitable activity, it will not be termed as partnership. 6. Liability of Partners:

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the 5 provisions of the Partnership Act that affect partnership accounts when the deed is silent.
cards.back:
Profit Sharing Ratio
Interest on Capital
Interest on Drawings
Interest on Loan
Remuneration for Firm’s Work
cards.quote: The important provisions affecting partnership accounts are as follows: (a) Profit Sharing Ratio: If the partnership deed is silent about the profit sharing ratio, the profits and losses of the firm are to be shared equally by partners, irrespective of their capital contribution in the firm. (b) Interest on Capital: No partner is entitled to claim any interest on the amount of capital contributed by him in the firm as a matter of right. However, interest can be allowed when it is expressly agreed to by the partners. Thus, no interest on capital is payable if the partnership deed is silent on the issue. (c) Interest on Drawings: No interest is to be charged on the drawings made by the partners, if there is no mention in the Deed. (d) Interest on Loan: If any partner has advanced loan to the firm for the purpose of business, he/she shall be entitled to get an interest on the loan amount at the rate of 6 per cent per annum. (e) Remuneration for Firm’s Work: No partner is entitled to get salary or other remuneration for taking part in the conduct of the business of the firm unless there is a provision for the same in the Partnership Deed.
