cards.front: Fixed amount withdrawn every month: for how many months is interest on the total amount calculated (beginning, end, middle of month)?
cards.back:
If withdrawn on the first day of every month, interest on total amount will be calculated for 6½ months
if withdrawn at the end at every month, it will be calculated for 5½ months
if withdrawn during the middle of the month, it will be calculated for 6 months
cards.quote: If withdrawn on the first day of every month, interest on total amount will be calculated for 6½ months; if withdrawn at the end at every month, it will be calculated for 5½ months, and if withdrawn during the middle of the month, it will be calculated for 6 months.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: When a fixed amount is withdrawn quarterly, on what does the total period depend?
cards.back: When fixed amount of money is withdrawn quarterly by partners, in such a situation, for the purpose of calculation of interest, the total period of time is ascertained depending on whether the money was withdrawn at the beginning or at the end of each quarter.
cards.quote: When fixed amount of money is withdrawn quarterly by partners, in such a situation, for the purpose of calculation of interest, the total period of time is ascertained depending on whether the money was withdrawn at the beginning or at the end of each quarter.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Fixed amount withdrawn at the beginning of each quarter: for what period is interest on the total amount calculated?
cards.back: Alternatively, the interest can be calculated on the total amount withdrawn during the accounting year, i.e. Rs. 1,20,000 for a period of 7½ months (12+9+6+3)/4.
cards.quote: Alternatively, the interest can be calculated on the total amount withdrawn during the accounting year, i.e. Rs. 1,20,000 for a period of 7½ months (12+9+6+3)/4.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.note: At the beginning of each quarter the average period is 7½ months.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: When is the product method used to calculate interest on drawings?
cards.back: When the partners withdraw different amounts of money at different time intervals, the interest is calculated using the product method.
cards.quote: When the partners withdraw different amounts of money at different time intervals, the interest is calculated using the product method.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Formula: interest on drawings by the product method.
cards.back: Interest = Sum of Products × Rate × 1/12
cards.quote: Interest = Sum of Products × Rate × 1/12

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Total drawings given but dates of withdrawal not specified: what period is taken?
cards.back: For calculation of interest, the period would be taken as six months, which is the average period assuming, that amount is withdrawn evenly in the middle of the month, throughout the year.
cards.quote: For calculation of interest, the period would be taken as six months, which is the average period assuming, that amount is withdrawn evenly in the middle of the month, throughout the year.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is a guarantee of profit to a partner?
cards.back: Sometimes a partner is admitted into the firm with a guarantee of certain minimum amount by way of his share of profits of the firm.
cards.quote: Sometimes a partner is admitted into the firm with a guarantee of certain minimum amount by way of his share of profits of the firm.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts
source.section: 1.6 Guarantee of Profit to a Partner

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Who may give the guarantee of a minimum profit to the new partner?
cards.back: Such assurance may be given by all the old partners in a certain ratio or by any of the old partners, individually to the new partner.
cards.quote: Such assurance may be given by all the old partners in a certain ratio or by any of the old partners, individually to the new partner.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts
source.section: 1.6 Guarantee of Profit to a Partner

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Who makes good the deficiency in a partner’s guaranteed profit, and in what ratio?
cards.back: If, in any year, the share of profits as calculated according to his profit sharing ratio is less than the guaranteed amount, the deficiency is made good by the guaranteeing partners’ in the agreed ratio which usually is the profit sharing ratio.
cards.quote: If, in any year, the share of profits as calculated according to his profit sharing ratio is less than the guaranteed amount, the deficiency is made good by the guaranteeing partners’ in the agreed ratio which usually is the profit sharing ratio.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What are past adjustments in partnership accounts?
cards.back: Sometimes a few omissions or errors in the recording of transactions or the preparation of summary statements are found after the final accounts have been prepared and the profits distributed among the partners.
cards.quote: Sometimes a few omissions or errors in the recording of transactions or the preparation of summary statements are found after the final accounts have been prepared and the profits distributed among the partners.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the omissions that may call for a past adjustment.
cards.back:
interest on capitals
interest on drawings
interest on partners’ loan
partner’s salary
partner’s commission
outstanding expenses
cards.quote: The omission may be in respect of interest on capitals, interest on drawings, interest on partners’ loan, partner’s salary, partner’s commission or outstanding expenses.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Types: ways of making a past adjustment instead of altering old accounts.
cards.back:
Profit and Loss Adjustment Account
directly in the capital accounts of the concerned partners
cards.quote: ‘Profit and Loss Adjustment Account’, or (b) directly in the capital accounts of the concerned partners.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Direct adjustment in capital accounts: what is worked out first?
cards.back: For direct adjustment in partners’ capital accounts first a statement to ascertain the net effect of omission on partners’ capital accounts will be worked out as follows and then the adjustment entries can be recorded.
cards.quote: For direct adjustment in partners’ capital accounts first a statement to ascertain the net effect of omission on partners’ capital accounts will be worked out as follows and then the adjustment entries can be recorded.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: On the retirement or death of a partner, the existing partnership deed ____, and in its place, a ____ needs to be framed
cards.back: On the retirement or death of a partner, the existing partnership deed comes to an end, and in its place, a new partnership deed needs to be framed
cards.quote: On the retirement or death of a partner, the existing partnership deed comes to an end, and in its place, a new partnership deed needs to be framed

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Sum due to a retiring/deceased partner includes: name items (i) to (v).
cards.quote: The sum due to the retiring partner (in case of retirement) and to the legal representatives/ executors (in case of death) includes: (i) credit balance of his capital account; (ii) credit balance of his current account (if any); (iii) his share of goodwill; (iv) his share of accumulated profits (reserves); (v) his share in the gain of revaluation of assets and liabilities;

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts
source.section: 3.1 Ascertaining the Amount Due to Retiring/ Deceased Partner

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Sum due to a retiring/deceased partner: name items (vi) to (viii), after the capital, goodwill and reserve items.
cards.quote: (vi) his share of profits up to the date of retirement/death; (vii) interest on his capital, if involved, up to the date of retirement/death; and (viii) salary/commission, if any, due to him up to the date of retirement/death.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts
source.section: 3.1 Ascertaining the Amount Due to Retiring/ Deceased Partner

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is retirement of an existing partner?
cards.back: It means withdrawal by a partner from the business of the firm which may be due to his bad health, old age or change in business interests.
cards.quote: It means withdrawal by a partner from the business of the firm which may be due to his bad health, old age or change in business interests.

source.book: Accountancy : Partnership Accounts
source.section: 2.1 Modes of Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the deductions that may have to be made from the retiring/deceased partner's share.
cards.quote: The following deductions, if any, may have to be made from his share: (i) debit balance of his current account (if any); (ii) his share of goodwill to be written off, if necessary; (iii) his share of accumulated losses; (iv) his share of loss on revaluation of assets and liabilities; (v) his share of loss up to the date of retirement/death; (vi) his drawings up to the date of retirement/death; (vii) interest on drawings, if involved, up to the date of retirement/death.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts
source.section: 3.1 Ascertaining the Amount Due to Retiring/ Deceased Partner

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Under what kind of partnership can a partner retire at any time?
cards.back: In fact a partner can retire any time if the partnership is at will.
cards.quote: In fact a partner can retire any time if the partnership is at will.

source.book: Accountancy : Partnership Accounts
source.section: 2.1 Modes of Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Name the 8 accounting aspects involved on retirement or death of a partner.
cards.quote: Thus, similar to admission, the various accounting aspects involved on retirement or death of a partner are as follows: 1. Ascertainment of new profit sharing ratio and gaining ratio; 2. Treatment of goodwill; 3. Revaluation of assets and liabilities; 4. Adjustment in respect of unrecorded assets and liabilities; 5. Distribution of accumulated profits and losses; 6. Ascertainment of share of profit or loss up to the date of retirement/death; 7. Adjustment of capital, if required; 8. Settlement of the amounts due to retired/deceased partner;

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts
source.section: 3.1 Ascertaining the Amount Due to Retiring/ Deceased Partner

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is the new profit sharing ratio (on retirement or death of a partner)?
cards.back: New profit sharing ratio is the ratio in which the remaining partners will share future profits after the retirement or death of any partner.
cards.quote: New profit sharing ratio is the ratio in which the remaining partners will share future profits after the retirement or death of any partner.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: On the death of a partner, when may the partnership stand reconstituted?
cards.back: Partnership may also stand reconstituted on death of a partner, if the remaining partners decide to continue the business of the firm as usual.
cards.quote: Partnership may also stand reconstituted on death of a partner, if the remaining partners decide to continue the business of the firm as usual.

source.book: Accountancy : Partnership Accounts
source.section: 2.1 Modes of Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: The new share of each of the remaining partner will consist of his ____ in the firm plus the share ____ from the retiring /deceased partner.
cards.back: The new share of each of the remaining partner will consist of his own share in the firm plus the share acquired from the retiring /deceased partner.
cards.quote: The new share of each of the remaining partner will consist of his own share in the firm plus the share acquired from the retiring /deceased partner.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: No information on how continuing partners acquire the outgoing partner's share: in what ratio is it assumed?
cards.back: it is assumed that they will acquire it in the old profit sharing ratio and so share the future profits in their old ratio.
cards.quote: In fact, in the absence of any information regarding profit sharing ratio in which the remaining partners acquire the share of retiring/deceased partner, it is assumed that they will acquire it in the old profit sharing ratio and so share the future profits in their old ratio.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Situation (a) for new profit sharing ratio: continuing partners acquire the share in the old ratio. Is a new ratio computed?
cards.back: normally, the continuing partners acquire the share of retiring or deceased partners in the old profit sharing ratio, and there is no need to compute the new profit sharing ratio among them, as it will be same as the old profit sharing ratio among them.
cards.quote: normally, the continuing partners acquire the share of retiring or deceased partners in the old profit sharing ratio, and there is no need to compute the new profit sharing ratio among them, as it will be same as the old profit sharing ratio among them.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Situation (b): continuing partners acquire the share in a proportion other than their old ratio. What follows?
cards.back: In that case, there is need to compute the new profit sharing ratio among them.
cards.quote: The continuing partners may acquire the share in the profits of the retiring/deceased partner in a proportion other than their old ratio, In that case, there is need to compute the new profit sharing ratio among them.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Formula: new share of a continuing partner.
cards.back: New share of Continuing Partner = Old Share + Acquired share from the Outgoing Partner
cards.quote: New share of Continuing Partner = Old Share + Acquired share from the Outgoing Partner

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.note: New share = old share plus the part of the outgoing partner's share the continuing partner takes over.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Situation (c): the continuing partners agree on a specified new profit sharing ratio. What is the new ratio?
cards.back: In that case the ratio so specified will be the new profit sharing ratio.
cards.quote: The contributing partners may agree on a specified new profit sharing ratio: In that case the ratio so specified will be the new profit sharing ratio.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: On retirement/death, who compensates the outgoing partner for his share of goodwill, and in what ratio?
cards.back: the retiring/ deceased partner compensated for his share of goodwill by the continuing partners (who have gained due to acquisition of share of profit from the retiring/ deceased partner) in their gaining ratio.
cards.quote: Hence, at the time of retirement/death of a partner, goodwill is valued as per agreement among the partners the retiring/ deceased partner compensated for his share of goodwill by the continuing partners (who have gained due to acquisition of share of profit from the retiring/ deceased partner) in their gaining ratio.

source.book: Accountancy – Partnership Accounts

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: Goodwill does not appear in the firm's books on retirement. How is credit given to the retiring partner?
cards.back: credit is given to the retiring partner for the share in goodwill by debiting the goodwill account to gaining partners capital accounts (individually) in their gaining ratio
cards.quote: When goodwill does not appear in the books of the firm, credit is given to the retiring partner for the share in goodwill by debiting the goodwill account to gaining partners capital accounts (individually) in their gaining ratio.

cards.back: his capital account will also be credited along with the retiring/deceased partner's capital account in proportion to his sacrifice and the other continuing partners' capital accounts will be debited based on their gain in the future profit ratio.
cards.quote: In such a situation his capital account will also be credited along with the retiring/deceased partner's capital account in proportion to his sacrifice and the other continuing partners' capital accounts will be debited based on their gain in the future profit ratio.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.front: What is hidden goodwill (retiring/deceased partner settled by a lump sum)?
cards.back: If the firm has agreed to settle the retiring or deceased partner's account by paying him a lump sum amount, then the amount paid to him in excess of what is due to him, based on the balance in his capital account after making necessary adjustments in respect of accumulated profits and losses and revaluation of assets and liabilities, etc., shall be treated as his share of goodwill (known as hidden goodwill).
cards.quote: If the firm has agreed to settle the retiring or deceased partner's account by paying him a lump sum amount, then the amount paid to him in excess of what is due to him, based on the balance in his capital account after making necessary adjustments in respect of accumulated profits and losses and revaluation of assets and liabilities, etc., shall be treated as his share of goodwill (known as hidden goodwill).

cards.front: Name the 7 features of a company.
cards.back:
Body Corporate
Separate Legal Entity
Limited Liability
Perpetual Succession
Common Seal
Transferability of Shares
May Sue or be Sued
cards.quote: Body Corporate: A company is formed according to the provisions of Law enforced from time to time. Generally, in India, the companies are formed and registered under Companies Law except in the case of Banking and Insurance companies for which a separate Law is provided for. • Separate Legal Entity: A company has a separate legal entity which is distinct and separate from its members. It can hold and deal with any type of property. It can enter into contracts and even open a bank account in its own name. • Limited Liability: The liability of the members of the company is limited to the extent of unpaid amount of the shares held by them. In the case of the companies limited by guarantee, the liability of its members is limited to the extent of the guarantee given by them in the event of the company being wound up. • Perpetual Succession: The company being an artificial person created by law continues to exist irrespective of the changes in its membership. A company can be terminated only through law. The death or insanity or insolvency of any member of the company in no way affects the existence of the company. Members may come and go but the company continues. • Common Seal: The company being an artificial person, cannot sign its name by itself. Therefore, every company is required to have its own seal which acts as official signatures of the company. Any document which does not carry the common seal of the company is not binding on the company. • Transferability of Shares: The shares of a public limited company are freely transferable. The permission of the company or the consent of any member of the company is not necessary for the transfer of shares. But the Articles of the company can prescribe the manner in which the transfer of shares will be made. • May Sue or be Sued: A company being a legal person can enter into contracts and can enforce the contractual rights against others. It can sue and be sued in its name if there is a breach of contract by the company.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Types of share capital (categories, from the accounting point of view).
cards.back:
Authorised Capital
Issued Capital
Subscribed Capital
Called up Capital
Paid up Capital
Uncalled Capital
Reserve Capital
cards.quote: Authorised Capital: Authorised capital is the amount of share capital which a company is authorised to issue by its Memorandum of Association. The company cannot raise more than the amount of capital as specified in the Memorandum of Association. It is also called Nominal or Registered capital. The authorised capital can be increased or decreased as per the procedure laid down in the Companies Act. It should be noted that the company need not issue the entire authorised capital for public subscription at a time. Depending upon its requirement, it may issue share capital but in any case, it should not be more than the amount of authorised capital. • Issued Capital: It is that part of the authorised capital which is actually issued to the public for subscription including the shares allotted to vendors and the signatories to the company’s memorandum. The authorised capital which is not offered for public subscription is known as ‘unissued capital’. Unissued capital may be offered for public subscription at a later date. • Subscribed Capital: It is that part of the issued capital which has been actually subscribed by the public. When the shares offered for public subscription are subscribed fully by the public the issued capital and subscribed capital would be the same. It may be noted that ultimately, the subscribed capital may be equal to or less than issued capital. In case the number of shares subscribed is less than what is offered, the company allots only the number of shares for which subscription has been received. In case it is higher than what is offered, the allotment will be equal to the offer. In other words, the fact of over subscription is not reflected in the books. • Called up Capital: It is that part of the subscribed capital which has been called up on the shares, i.e., what the company has asked the shareholders to pay. The company may decide to call the entire amount or part of the face value of the shares, For example, if the face value (also called nominal value) of a share allotted is Rs. 10 and the company has called up only Rs. 7 per share, in that scenario, the called up capital is Rs. 7 per share. The remaining Rs. 3 may be collected from its shareholders as and when needed. • Paid up Capital: It is that portion of the called up capital which has been actually received from the shareholders. When the shareholders have paid all the called amount, the called up capital is the same to the paid up capital. If any of the shareholders has not paid amount on calls, such an amount may be called as ‘calls in arrears’. Therefore, paid up capital is equal to the called-up capital minus call in arrears. • Uncalled Capital: That portion of the subscribed capital which has not yet been called up. As stated earlier, the company may collect this amount any time when it needs further funds. • Reserve Capital: A company may reserve a portion of its uncalled capital to be called only in the event of winding up of the company. Such uncalled amount is called ‘Reserve Capital’ of the company. It is available only for the creditors on winding up of the company.

cards.back: A company may reserve a portion of its uncalled capital to be called only in the event of winding up of the company. Such uncalled amount is called 'Reserve Capital' of the company.
cards.quote: A company may reserve a portion of its uncalled capital to be called only in the event of winding up of the company. Such uncalled amount is called 'Reserve Capital' of the company.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Reserve Capital: for whom is it available on winding up of the company?
cards.back:
Only for the creditors
It is available only for the creditors on winding up of the company.
cards.quote: It is available only for the creditors on winding up of the company.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What is a share?
cards.back: Shares, refer to the units into which the total share capital of a company is divided. Thus, a share is a fractional part of the share capital and forms the basis of ownership interest in a company.
cards.quote: Shares, refer to the units into which the total share capital of a company is divided. Thus, a share is a fractional part of the share capital and forms the basis of ownership interest in a company.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Types of shares a company can issue under the Companies Act.
cards.back: As per The Companies Act, a company can issue two types of shares (1) preference shares, and (2) equity shares (also called ordinary shares).
cards.quote: As per The Companies Act, a company can issue two types of shares (1) preference shares, and (2) equity shares (also called ordinary shares).

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Name the 2 conditions a preference share fulfils (Section 43, Companies Act, 2013).
cards.back:
(a) That it carries a preferential right to dividend to be paid either as a fixed amount payable to preference shareholders or an amount calculated by a fixed rate of the nominal value of each share before any dividend is paid to the equity shareholders.
(b) That with respect to capital it carries or will carry, on the winding up of the company, the preferential right to the repayment of capital before anything is paid to equity shareholders.
cards.quote:
(a) That it carries a preferential right to dividend to be paid either as a fixed amount payable to preference shareholders or an amount calculated by a fixed rate of the nominal value of each share before any dividend is paid to the equity shareholders.
(b) That with respect to capital it carries or will carry, on the winding up of the company, the preferential right to the repayment of capital before anything is paid to equity shareholders.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Types of preference shares.
cards.back: Thus, the preference shares can be participating and nonparticipating. Similarly, these shares can be cumulative or non-cumulative, and redeemable or irredeemable.
cards.quote: Thus, the preference shares can be participating and nonparticipating. Similarly, these shares can be cumulative or non-cumulative, and redeemable or irredeemable.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Define equity share (Section 43, Companies Act, 2013).
cards.back: an equity share is a share which is not a preference share.
cards.quote: an equity share is a share which is not a preference share.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: The equity shareholders are entitled to share the ____ of the company after satisfying the dividend rights of the preference share holders.
cards.back: The equity shareholders are entitled to share the distributable profits of the company after satisfying the dividend rights of the preference share holders.
cards.quote: The equity shareholders are entitled to share the distributable profits of the company after satisfying the dividend rights of the preference share holders.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What is a prospectus?
cards.back: Prospectus is an invitation to the public that a new company has come into existence and it needs funds for doing business.
cards.quote: Prospectus is an invitation to the public that a new company has come into existence and it needs funds for doing business.

cards.back: Disclosure of shares in the company held by each shareholder holding more than 5% shares specifying the number of shares held.

cards.front: The first instalment is collected along with application and is thus, known as ____, the second on allotment (termed as ____)
cards.back: The first instalment is collected along with application and is thus, known as application money, the second on allotment (termed as allotment money)
cards.quote: The first instalment is collected along with application and is thus, known as application money, the second on allotment (termed as allotment money)

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Within how many days of the prospectus issue must minimum subscription be received?
cards.back: The company has to get minimum subscription within 120 days from the date of the issue of the prospectus.
cards.quote: The company has to get minimum subscription within 120 days from the date of the issue of the prospectus.

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: If minimum subscription is not received, within how many days is application money returned?
cards.back: If the company fails to receive the same within the said period, the company cannot proceed for the allotment of shares and application money should be returned within 130 days of the date of issue of prospectus.
cards.quote: If the company fails to receive the same within the said period, the company cannot proceed for the allotment of shares and application money should be returned within 130 days of the date of issue of prospectus.

cards.front: What is the least minimum subscription, as a percentage of the issued amount (SEBI guidelines)?
cards.back: 'minimum subscription' of capital cannot be less than 90% of the issued amount according to SEBI (Disclosure and Investor Protection) Guidelines, 2000

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Delay in refund beyond how many days from closure of the subscription list incurs interest, and at what rate?
cards.back:
8 days; interest at 15%
If a delay occurs beyond 8 days from the date of closure of subscription list, the company shall be liable to pay the amount with interest at the rate of 15% [Section 73(2)].
cards.quote: If a delay occurs beyond 8 days from the date of closure of subscription list, the company shall be liable to pay the amount with interest at the rate of 15% [Section 73(2)].

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: When are shares issued at par?
cards.back: Shares are to be issued at par when their issue price is exactly equal to their nominal value according to the terms and conditions of issue.
cards.quote: Shares are to be issued at par when their issue price is exactly equal to their nominal value according to the terms and conditions of issue.

cards.front: What is premium on shares?
cards.back: When the shares of a company are issued more than its nominal value (face value), the excess amount is called premium.

Second, there must be an interval of at least one month between the making of two calls unless otherwise provided by the articles of association of the company.

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What is Over Subscription?
cards.back: There are instances when applications for more shares of a company are received than the number offered to the public for subscription. This usually happens in respect of shares issue of well-managed and financially strong companies and is said to be a case of 'Over Subscription'.
cards.quote: There are instances when applications for more shares of a company are received than the number offered to the public for subscription. This usually happens in respect of shares issue of well-managed and financially strong companies and is said to be a case of 'Over Subscription'.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Three alternatives open to directors in case of over subscription.
cards.quote: (1) they can accept some applications in full and totally reject the others; (2) they can make a pro-rata allotment to all; and (3) they can adopt a combination of the above two alternatives which happens to be the most common course adopted in practice.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: First alternative in over subscription: what happens to the money on rejected applications?
cards.back:
It is fully refunded
When the directors decide to fully accept some applications and totally reject the others, the application money received on rejected applications is fully refunded.
cards.quote: When the directors decide to fully accept some applications and totally reject the others, the application money received on rejected applications is fully refunded.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: When the directors opt to make a proportionate allotment to all applicants (called '____' allotment)
cards.back: When the directors opt to make a proportionate allotment to all applicants (called 'pro-rata' allotment)
cards.quote: When the directors opt to make a proportionate allotment to all applicants (called 'pro-rata' allotment)

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: (called 'pro-rata' allotment), the excess application money received is normally adjusted towards the ____.
cards.back: (called 'pro-rata' allotment), the excess application money received is normally adjusted towards the amount due on allotment.
cards.quote: (called 'pro-rata' allotment), the excess application money received is normally adjusted towards the amount due on allotment.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Pro-rata allotment: if excess application money exceeds the amount due on allotment, what may be done with it?
cards.back:
Refunded, or credited to calls in advance
In case, the excess application money received is more than the amount due on allotment of shares, such excess amount may either be refunded or credited to calls in advance.
cards.quote: In case, the excess application money received is more than the amount due on allotment of shares, such excess amount may either be refunded or credited to calls in advance.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Third alternative in over subscription: treatment of rejected and of excess application money?
cards.back: When the application for some shares are rejected outrightly; and pro-rata allotment is made to the remaining applicants, the money on rejected applications is refunded and the excess application money received from applicants to whom pro-rata allotment has been made is adjusted towards the amount due on the allotment of shares allotted.
cards.quote: When the application for some shares are rejected outrightly; and pro-rata allotment is made to the remaining applicants, the money on rejected applications is refunded and the excess application money received from applicants to whom pro-rata allotment has been made is adjusted towards the amount due on the allotment of shares allotted.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: What is Under Subscription?
cards.back: Under subscription is a situation where number of shares applied for is less than the number for which applications have been invited for subscription.
cards.quote: Under subscription is a situation where number of shares applied for is less than the number for which applications have been invited for subscription.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements

cards.front: What is the issue of shares at a premium?
cards.back: It is quite common for the shares of financially strong and well-managed companies to be issued at a premium, i.e. at an amount more than the nominal or par value of shares.
cards.quote: It is quite common for the shares of financially strong and well-managed companies to be issued at a premium, i.e. at an amount more than the nominal or par value of shares.

cards.back: Thus, when a share of the nominal value of Rs. 100 is issued at Rs. 105, it is said to have been issued at a premium of 5 per cent.
cards.quote: Thus, when a share of the nominal value of Rs. 100 is issued at Rs. 105, it is said to have been issued at a premium of 5 per cent.

cards.front: Shares issued at a premium: with which amount is the premium generally called?
cards.back:
Generally with the amount due on allotment
However, premium is generally called with the amount due on allotment, sometimes with the application money and rarely with the call money.
cards.quote: However, premium is generally called with the amount due on allotment, sometimes with the application money and rarely with the call money.

source.book: Accountancy Part 2: Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements
source.section: 1.6.5 Issue of Shares at a Premium

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Securities Premium can be used only for which 5 purposes?
cards.quote: (a) to issue fully paid bonus shares to the extent not exceeding unissued share capital of the company; (b) to write-off preliminary expenses of the company; (c) to write-off the expenses of, or commission paid, or discount allowed on any securities of the company; and (d) to pay premium on the redemption of preference shares or debentures of the company. (e) Purchase of its own shares (i.e., buy back of shares).

cards.front: What is the issue of shares at a discount?
cards.back: There are instances when the shares of a company are issued at a discount, i.e. at an amount less than the nominal or par value of shares, the difference between the nominal value and issue price representing discount on the issue of shares.

cards.back:
Number of shares to be issued = Amount Payable / Issue Price
the number of shares to be issued will depend upon the price at which the shares are issued and the amount payable to the vendor
cards.quote: There are instances where a company enters into an arrangement with the vendors from whom it has purchased assets, whereby the latter agrees to accept, the payment in the form of fully paid shares of the company issued to them. Normally, no such cash is received for issue of shares. These shares can also be issued either at par, at premium or at discount, and the number of shares to be issued will depend upon the price at which the shares are issued and the amount payable to the vendor. cards.front: When shares are forfeited, which entry is not reversed?
cards.back:
The entry relating to share premium received, if any
It may be noted here that when the shares are forfeited, all entries relating to the forfeited shares must be reversed except the entry relating to share premium received, if any.
cards.quote: It may be noted here that when the shares are forfeited, all entries relating to the forfeited shares must be reversed except the entry relating to share premium received, if any.

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: On forfeiture, share capital is debited to the extent of called-up capital and credited to which two accounts?
cards.back:
Unpaid calls (calls in arrears) and Share Forfeiture account
Accordingly, the share capital is debited to the extent to called-up capital and credited to (i) respective unpaid calls account i.e., calls in arrears and (ii) share forfeiture account with the amount already received on shares.
cards.quote: Accordingly, the share capital is debited to the extent to called-up capital and credited to (i) respective unpaid calls account i.e., calls in arrears and (ii) share forfeiture account with the amount already received on shares.

cards.front: Shares forfeited, premium already received: is the securities premium account debited at forfeiture?
cards.back:
No, it is not debited at the time of forfeiture
The important point to be noted in this context is that the securities premium account is not to be debited at the time of forfeiture if the premium has been received in respect of the forefeited shares
cards.quote: The important point to be noted in this context is that the securities premium account is not to be debited at the time of forfeiture if the premium has been received in respect of the forefeited shares

cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Shares forfeited, premium not received: which account is also debited with the premium not received?
cards.back:
Securities Premium Reserve Account
In case, however, if the premium amount has not been received, either wholly or partially, in respect of the shares forfeited, the Securities Premium Reserve Account will also be debited with the amount of premium not received along with the Share Capital Account at the time forfeiture.

cards.front: Is it mandatory for a company to maintain a separate Calls-in-Arrears Account?
cards.back:

cards.subject: accountancy
cards.unit: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
cards.front: Calls in arrears and calls in advance: does the company charge or pay interest on each?
cards.back:
Arrears: power to charge; advance: obligation to pay
A company has the power to charge interest on calls in arrears and is under an obligation to pay interest on calls-in-advance if it accepts them in accordance with the provisions of Articles of Association.

cards.front: If all forfeited shares are not reissued, how much of the Share Forfeiture balance goes to capital reserve?
cards.back: In the event of all forfeited share not being reissued, the credit amount on Share forfeiture account relating to shares yet to be reissued is carried forward and the remaining balance on the account only is credited to capital reserve account.
